sentences.text: Indosinosuchus is an extinct genus of teleosaurid crocodylomorph that lived in Thailand during the Jurassic.
All of its teeth were slender, conical, and featured curved crowns.
The animal possessed wider-than-long osteoderms in its trunk and longer-than-wide subrectangular osteoderms on its tail, all bearing a front-to-back keel.
The genus Indosinosuchus was formally described by Martin and colleagues in 2019.
Material for the species Indosinosuchus peninsularensis was collected from the Ban Nam Pun site in 2004.
Fossils of this species have been found in Thailand, specifically within the Khlong Min Formation.
While the type species of Indosinosuchus is known from freshwater environments, I. peninsularensis is considered a marine species.
Indosinosuchus evolved convergent adaptations with machimosaurids, including robust jaws and strong muscle attachments.

Indosinosuchus potamosiamensis possessed a strong bite comparable to derived machimosaurids due to well-developed lower jaw musculature and had the highest posterior mechanical advantage among all known teleosaurs.
Indosinosuchus peninsularensis is classified as a member of the family Teleosauridae.

In a 2019 study, Indosinosuchus was initially classified as a close relative or sister taxon of Machimosaurus hugii, but later analyses separated them into different families, teleosaurids and machimosaurids, respectively.
Indosinosuchus peninsularensis lived during the Middle to Late Jurassic period.
Indosinosuchus lived during the Late Jurassic or Early Cretaceous in what is now Thailand.
Indosinosuchus potamosiamensis is one of the few confirmed purely freshwater teleosaurs, with fossils found at the Phu Noi locality representing an oxbow lake or abandoned river channel.
The precise age of Indosinosuchus is debated, with vertebrate fossils suggesting a Late Jurassic age and palynological data suggesting an Early Cretaceous age.
The validity of Indosinosuchus kalasinensis as a distinct species was questioned in a 2026 study by Lauprasert et al., who argued it was synonymous with I. potamosiamensis.
Researchers suggest that the lack of preserved postcranial material for I. kalasinensis may explain why phylogenetic studies fail to recover a clear relationship between its species.
There is a debate over whether differences between I. potamosiamensis and I. kalasinensis represent distinct ecological niches or are due to post-mortem skull distortion.
